newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICAN LAND CLAIM REACHES DEEP INTO HISTORY.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICAN LAND CLAIM REACHES DEEP INTO HISTORY.

text.p: Members of South Africa's Griqua community are claiming billions of rand from the British crown and the De Beers mining company, saying they were cheated and dispossessed by colonialists in the last century.
The Griqua People's Organisation (GPO) has sent the claims to the country's highest court, the Constitutional Court, but a court spokeswoman said on Tuesday they had come to the wrong place.
"We haven't issued them a case number," the spokeswoman said. "It's not the kind of case we would deal with."
The Griquas trace their ancestry to the late 18th and early 19th centuries when Dutch settlers moving into the interior intermarried with the orginal Khoi or Bushman inhabitants.

The GPO, one of several groups representing the Griquas who now live mainly in Northern Cape province, said in their claim they want 8.7 billion rand ($1.9 billion) from De Beers Consolidated Mines Ltd and 1.38 billion sterling ($1.9 billion) from the British crown.

The group said De Beers owed them money for the diamonds recovered over the years from what it said was Griqua land in the Kimberley region and Britain owed them for having violated colonial-era pacts and for "psychic abuse and loss of ethnic identity".
De Beers has rejected the GPO position.
"The grounds which apparently give rise to their claims for restitution and compensation predate the formation of this company in 1888," a company statement said.

"We would like to stress that De Beers acquired its properties and mineral rights holdings from the previous lawful holders," it said. "De Beers denies that at any time it dispossessed the Griqua people or anyone else of any land or mineral rights."
A spokesman for the British High Commission said the GPO had been in touch, but he declined to give details.
Another Griqua group, the Griqua National Conference (GNC), said it supported the idea of obtaining rights for the community but felt the GPO was going about it in the wrong way.
"We do not agree with the confrontational approach," said GNC legal representative Mansell Upham. "It should be done in a responsible way in terms of the legitimate claims of the Griquas."
The GNC is up in arms at what it regards as insensitive treatment by the African National Congress government of President Nelson Mandela.

The group has refused to cooperate with the national census now being carried out, saying census forms make no provision for the Griquas as an ethnic group in their own right. The group says the government is trying to lump Griquas with coloureds, the racial classification applied to South Africans of mixed race.
South African economist Tony Twine said the GPO seemed to have little hope of success in their claims, but would set an interesting legal precedent it they did win.
"WWho would then own Manhattan, Sydney harbour and the City of London?" he asked.
